title: Your baptism day
hook: remember the day you began, or choose a day to mark
tomorrow: your phone sums up your year. what would a giving recap show?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two honest answers about holy places, and one road both keep: walk to pray. Today, a day that some Christians can't remember at all.
screen: `WALK TO PRAY.` → `A DAY YOU MIGHT NOT REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Nobody remembers being born. The cake and the candles every year are other people telling you: that day happened, and you're ours. Some Christians can say the same about baptism. Water on a baby's head, a name said aloud, and then years of hearing the story. Others remember every second: cold water, wet clothes, a church cheering. Either way, it's a birthday of a kind, and the water came first.
screen: `NOBODY REMEMBERS BEING BORN.` → `WATER, AND A NAME.` → `A BIRTHDAY OF A KIND.`

segments.voice: Start where Jesus starts. Mark says that as he came up out of the water, the heavens opened and a voice said: “Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” He hasn't preached or healed anyone yet. The love comes before the work. Paul says baptism joins a person to that story: “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” Like a coat you put on every morning. To the Romans he calls it a burial and a rising, so that “we also should walk in newness of life.” Christians differ here, and both sides care deeply. Some churches baptize babies, so the day is a gift received before memory. Others baptize those old enough to ask for it, so the day is a choice remembered. Isaiah's words fit either one: “Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in Mark, the first thing said to Jesus after the water isn't a job to do. It's a name: beloved. So a baptism day isn't mainly about remembering an event. It's remembering whose you are. If you know your date, you can keep it. If not, you can ask family or the church, or choose a day to mark.
screen: `BELOVED, BEFORE ANY WORK.` · `PUT ON CHRIST, LIKE A COAT.` · `A BABY, OR ONE WHO ASKS.` · `THOU ART MINE.` · then, large: `REMEMBER WHOSE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Set a glass or bowl of water in front of you, or stand at a tap. Touch the water with your fingertips and notice it: cool, wet, ordinary. If you pray, you can hear Isaiah's last words as you touch it, thou art mine; if not, rest your wet hands in your lap and feel them slowly dry.
Your baptism day. The day the water came, remembered or chosen and marked, as a way of remembering whose you are.
Keep this one: remember whose you are, which was settled before anything you did. Day seventeen-twelve, with water still on your hands.

howItsDone: Some churches baptize infants and others baptize those old enough to ask; some Christians keep the date each year, and some touch water as a reminder, such as holy water at a church door or a renewal of baptismal promises.

fork.setup: your cousin was baptized at fifteen and remembers every second. you were a baby. she says hers "counts more." what fits today's lesson?
options: hers counts more, because a choice beats a gift.
yours counts more, because earlier is better.

chat.says: leader said touch the lake and 'remember your baptism.' i was a BABY. does that even count?
options: Churches differ about babies, but either way it marks whose you are, not what you remember.
Only if you know the exact date. Without the date there's nothing to remember.
It's just a family custom. The lake thing is a nice feeling, nothing more.
chat.meaning: Some churches baptize babies, others those who ask. Either way, at Jesus' baptism 'beloved' came first: a baptism day remembers whose you are.

baptism.meaning: a washing with water that marks a person as Christ's
